flaw.ctx: The assistant produced this. Later a user reported: "Distance is right, but the queue holds about twice as many entries as there are cells."
flaw.answer: Cells are marked visited on **dequeue**, so a cell can be enqueued once per neighbour before it is processed. **7,081 enqueues for 3,600 cells** on a 60×60 grid; on a word graph with ~25 neighbours per node the factor is ~25×.

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> LinkedIn has users connected to other users.
> 
> Given:
> 
> interface Member {
>     int getMemberId();
>     List<Member> getConnections();
> }
> 
> Find the shortest connection distance between two members.
> 
> Example:
> 
> Bob -> Alice -> Frank
> 
> Distance(Bob, Frank) = 2

**Given with it:** What if one member has a very large connection size while the other has a small connection size?

The social graph, reachable only through an interface: given a member you can ask for its id and its connections. There is no adjacency matrix, no id-to-member map, no global view. You discover the graph by walking it.

The number of hops on the shortest path between two members, or a sentinel if they are in different components. The supplied example fixes hops, not people: 2 for Bob→Alice→Frank.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Ids are unique and stable. | They are the identity for the visited set. If two distinct members could share an id the search would silently prune real paths. |
| `GetConnections()` may return null or contain nulls. | A real interface like this usually does eventually. Guarding costs two lines and turns a crash into a correct answer. |
| Distance counts edges. Self is 0, a direct connection is 1. | Pinned by the supplied example. If they wanted people counted it is +1 everywhere — confirm which, because "degree of connection" in the LinkedIn product means edges. |
| `GetConnections()` is cheap and local. | It is not, in reality — it is a service call. That assumption is exactly what the distributed follow-up removes, and naming it early sets that up. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The first observation is that there is nothing to invent: shortest path on an unweighted graph is BFS, and BFS is optimal here. Saying that quickly and moving on is the right use of the first thirty seconds.

The second observation is the one the question is actually built around, and it is in the follow-up. **The cost of a BFS round is the size of the frontier you expand, and if you search from both ends you get to choose which frontier that is.** A single BFS to depth `d` touches roughly `b^d` nodes, where b is the branching factor. Two searches meeting in the middle touch about `2 · b^(d/2)`. At LinkedIn’s average connection count that is not a constant factor — at b = 500 and d = 4 it is 62 billion versus half a million.

Now the lopsided part. If one member has 30,000 connections and the other has 40, expanding the hub first costs 30,000 node visits to advance one level; expanding the small side costs 40. They meet at the same place either way. So the rule is: **each round, expand whichever frontier is currently smaller.** Not "start from the smaller one" — re-decide every round, because the small side may become the large one after it touches a hub.

That is the answer to the supplied follow-up, and it is one `if` plus a swap.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Depth-first search from the source, recording the length of every path that reaches the target, then take the minimum. *Exponential in the worst case. Even with a visited set, DFS finds *a* path and it is not necessarily the shortest, so pruning by visited is unsound.*

**Why not good enough.** This is the mistake worth naming explicitly, because it is a correctness error and not a performance one. DFS with a visited set returns the first path it stumbles onto, which can be arbitrarily longer than the shortest. To make DFS correct you must allow revisiting nodes at shorter depths, and then you are exploring exponentially many paths. BFS avoids both problems at once: it visits by increasing distance, so the first time it reaches a node is the shortest way to reach it, which is what licenses the visited set.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | Two `IMember` references. No global view of the graph. |
| TRANSFORMATION | Nothing is precomputed. Neighbours come from `GetConnections()` on demand. |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Queue<IMember>` for the frontier and `HashSet<int>` for visited ids. For the bidirectional version, two frontiers as `Dictionary<int, IMember>` and two visited sets. |
| ALGORITHM | Level-by-level BFS, incrementing depth once per level. Bidirectional: expand the smaller frontier each round and stop when a node is in the other side’s visited set. |
| OUTPUT | Hops, or -1 if unreachable |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Handle the trivial cases: either null → -1; same id → 0.
- Seed the frontier with the source and mark its id visited.
- Take the whole current level. Increment `depth`.
- For each node in the level, for each connection: if it is the target, return `depth`.
- Otherwise, if the id is new, mark it and add it to the next level.
- Repeat until the queue empties, then return -1.
- **Bidirectional:** maintain two frontiers; each round swap so `frontA` is the smaller, expand it, and return `depth` as soon as a discovered id is in `seenB`.

- Connections are **unweighted**, so BFS is optimal and Dijkstra would be pointless overhead. Say that — reaching for Dijkstra here is a recognisable tell.
- The graph is undirected in practice (a connection is mutual on LinkedIn) but the interface does not promise it. The algorithm works either way; only the bidirectional version cares.
- Visited must be tracked by **id**, not by object reference. Nothing guarantees that the same member arrives as the same instance twice, and `Equals` is not specified on the interface.
- The graph is enormous. The follow-up about lopsided connection counts is really about this.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `HashSet<int>` keyed by id | O(1) membership, and keyed on the only identity the interface guarantees. Using the member object would depend on `Equals` and `GetHashCode` that the interface never promises. |
| Level-by-level, not a queue of `(node, depth)` pairs | Both are correct. Levelling is less state and makes the "distance is edges" convention visible in the code — `depth++` happens exactly once per level, so there is one place to check the off-by-one. |
| `Dictionary<int, IMember>` for the bidirectional frontiers | A frontier must be countable (to decide which side to expand) and membership-testable (to detect the meeting). A dictionary does both; a queue does neither. |
| Two separate visited sets | The meeting test is "is this id in the **other** side’s visited set". One shared set would make the two searches prune each other and report the wrong distance. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`int levelSize = queue.Count;` before the inner loop.** Captured **before** the loop, because the loop enqueues into the same queue. Reading `queue.Count` inside the condition would consume the next level in the same round and return a distance that is too small. This is the classic level-BFS bug and it produces a plausible wrong number rather than a crash.

**Why the target check is on discovery, not on dequeue.** Checking `next == to` as soon as the edge is seen returns `depth` one round earlier than waiting to dequeue it. Both are correct if the bookkeeping matches; checking on discovery means `depth` has already been incremented for this level, which is exactly the number of edges traversed. Checking on dequeue with the same `depth++` placement would be off by one.

**The tuple swap in the bidirectional version.** `(frontA, frontB) = (frontB, frontA);` together with the visited sets. Swapping the frontiers without swapping the visited sets would test membership against the wrong side and silently return nonsense — the two lines must move together, which is why they are adjacent.

**Why `depth++` is right despite the swapping.** Each round advances exactly one edge, whichever side was expanded. The depth is the total number of edges laid down by both searches combined, and the meeting point is the last edge. This is the part I would not trust on inspection, which is why the test suite cross-checks both implementations on 120 random pairs.

**`seen.Add(id)` as the test.** `HashSet.Add` returns false if the element was present, so the membership test and the insertion are one operation. Two calls would be correct and would give a second place for the two to disagree.

**Nulls, twice.** `cur.GetConnections() ?? new List<IMember>()` and `if (nb == null) continue;`. The interface promises neither, and a graph served from a real backend will eventually hand you both.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Distance` (BFS) | O(V + E) worst case, O(b^d) typical | O(V) | Every node enqueued once, every edge examined once |
| `DistanceBidirectional` | O(b^(d/2)) typical | O(b^(d/2)) | Two shallow searches instead of one deep one |
| lopsided case | O(small^d) rather than O(large^d) | same | Expanding the smaller frontier each round |

**The bidirectional win is not a constant factor.** With branching factor b and distance d, one search touches b^d and two touch 2b^(d/2). At b = 500, d = 4: about 62 billion against about 500,000. That is the number to have ready, because "it is about twice as fast" is the wrong intuition and a common one. The space also drops, which matters more here than the time — a single BFS frontier at depth 3 in a social graph does not fit in memory.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Either member null | Returns -1 rather than throwing. Debatable; state which you chose. |
| Same member | 0, handled before the search starts. |
| Direct connection | 1. Worth testing explicitly — it is the off-by-one case. |
| No path | -1 in both implementations. The bidirectional version must exit when **either** frontier empties, not both. |
| A cycle | Handled by the visited set. Without it, BFS on a social graph does not terminate. |
| `GetConnections()` returns null | Treated as empty. |
| A self-connection | The id is already in `seen`, so it is skipped. |
| One member with 30,000 connections | The supplied follow-up. Bidirectional expands the other side and never enumerates the hub. |
| Both members are hubs | Bidirectional still helps, because the *depth* halves even when neither side is small. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**What if one member has a very large connection size while the other has a small connection size?**

Bidirectional BFS, expanding whichever frontier is currently smaller each round. Keep two visited sets and stop when a newly discovered id appears in the other side’s set. One `if` and a swap on top of plain BFS.

*Trade-off:* Two frontiers and two visited sets instead of one, and the code is genuinely harder to get right — the depth accounting and the swap are both easy to break, and the failure is a wrong number rather than a crash. In exchange you go from b^d to b^(d/2), which is the difference between fitting in memory and not. It also requires the graph to be traversable **backwards**; on LinkedIn connections are mutual so that is free, but on a directed graph like follows you would need a reverse index.

**Return the path, not just the distance.**

Keep a `Dictionary<int, IMember> parent` alongside the visited set and walk it back from the target. For the bidirectional version you need two parent maps and must join them at the meeting node, reversing one side — and that is the part that gets fumbled, because the meeting node belongs to both.

*Trade-off:* O(V) extra memory for the parent map, which in a social graph is the same order as the visited set you already have, so it is nearly free. Storing the full path per frontier node instead of a parent pointer is the tempting version and multiplies memory by the path length.

**Cap it at 3 degrees, which is what the product actually shows.**

Stop expanding past depth 3 and return "3+" or "out of network". With bidirectional search each side only ever goes to depth 2, which bounds the work hard regardless of hubs.

*Trade-off:* This is the one that turns an intractable graph query into a serveable one. It is also a product decision disguised as an optimisation — LinkedIn shows 1st, 2nd, 3rd and "out of network" precisely because the fourth degree is both unhelpful to a user and unaffordable to compute. Saying that connection out loud is a strong signal.

**The graph does not fit on one machine. How is this actually served?**

Two things. Batch the frontier: one request per **level**, asking for the connections of every node in the frontier at once, rather than one request per node. That turns d round trips out of b^d. And partition the graph by member id with the adjacency list co-located, so a level expansion is a scatter-gather across partitions.

For first-degree and second-degree, precompute. Second-degree sets are large but bounded and change slowly, so a bloom filter or a compressed set per member answers "are we within 2" without any traversal at all — which is what makes the badge on a profile page instant.

*Trade-off:* Batching is a pure win and is the first thing to do. Precomputation trades storage and staleness for latency: a bloom filter gives false positives, so "2nd degree" might occasionally be wrong in the optimistic direction, which for a badge is an acceptable error and for an access-control decision would not be.

**Why not Dijkstra, or A*?**

Dijkstra solves weighted shortest path. All edges here have weight 1, and on a unit-weight graph Dijkstra degenerates into BFS with a priority queue bolted on — same answer, worse constant, `O(log V)` per operation for nothing. A* needs an admissible heuristic estimating distance-to-target, and in a social graph there is no coordinate to estimate from.

*Trade-off:* If connections were weighted — interaction strength, say — Dijkstra becomes correct and BFS becomes wrong. That is the condition to state, rather than dismissing Dijkstra outright.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Time and space complexity? Can it be improved? What happens as N grows?* — States both, names the bottleneck
